citations.context: And importantly, when Jonah proclaims God's judgment upon Nineveh, the text does not record any suggestion that Nineveh might avoid the judgment. Indeed, the judgment appears categorical. Forty more days and Nineveh shall be under overthrown. But Jonah knows better than to think that the proclamation of God's judgment would seal the deal for Nineveh, for he knows that God cares for the Ninevehes. If anything, Jonah is the retributivist here, and he by no means represents the view endorsed by the book regarding God's justice.

citations.context: Consider the book of Jonah, in which we see the titular prophet fleeing to Tarshus in hopes of escaping his prophetic call. Toward the end of the book, Jonah gives us a direct explanation for why he initially fled God's call. He writes, Jonah prayed to the Lord and said, O Lord, is not this what I said while I was still in my own country? That's why I fled to Tarshus at the beginning, for I knew that you are a gracious and merciful God, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from punishment.
